question: A person asks: 'My company has a policy requiring employees to log all hours worked, including overtime, in a timesheet system. Last week I worked two extra hours on a project but did not log them at the time. I could add them to this week's timesheet instead, attributing them to a current project that is similar. The total hours would still be accurate. Is this ethically acceptable?'

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The timesheet policy exists so that labor costs are accurately attributed to projects and that employees are properly compensated. If the two hours genuinely occurred and you are entitled to be paid for them, recording them produces the correct outcome: accurate compensation and a true total count of hours worked. The concern is about project attribution — recording last week's hours under this week's project introduces a small inaccuracy in how costs are allocated between projects. Whether that matters depends on how the data is used. If project-level cost tracking is important to your organization, the better approach is to correct last week's record directly or flag the discrepancy to your manager, so the attribution is accurate, not just the total.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: Timesheets are records, and accuracy in records is a straightforward honesty matter. Attributing last week's hours to this week's project — even if the total is correct — produces a record that does not accurately reflect when the work happened or which project it belonged to. A person who values honesty in their work keeps accurate records, including when it requires the minor inconvenience of correcting a past entry or explaining an error to a manager. The right move is to correct last week's timesheet directly, or to speak with your manager about how to handle the late entry. Adjusting this week's record to absorb the discrepancy quietly is a small inaccuracy, but it is still an inaccuracy you would be choosing to introduce.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: Timesheet records are factual documents, and entering last week's hours under this week's project would make the record inaccurate — regardless of whether the total hours are correct. Your organization's policy requires logging hours as they occur and attributing them to the correct project. Retroactively shifting hours between weeks and projects to correct an oversight, without disclosure, does not comply with that policy even if the intent is benign. The correct course is to amend last week's timesheet with an explanatory note, or to ask your manager how late entries should be handled. Following the policy as it is intended — accurate attribution, not just accurate totals — is what your employment agreement calls for.

chat_history.text: {"question":"A software developer asks: 'Our team has a code review policy requiring at least two approvals before merging any pull request. I have a small one-line bug fix that is clearly correct — it just changes a variable name that was misspelled. My two usual reviewers are both in a long meeting. I could wait a few hours, or I could merge it now since the fix is obviously right and low risk. What should I think about here from an ethical standpoint?'","reference_answers":[{"key":"expected_utilitarian","text":"The ethical weight here comes down to what outcomes the two-approval policy actually produces. The policy exists to catch errors, ensure shared understanding of the codebase, and distribute responsibility for changes. For a genuinely trivial one-character typo fix, the error-catching function is largely already satisfied by your own careful review — the marginal benefit of two additional approvals is very small. Against that, the cost is a few hours of delay on a fix that may matter to users or colleagues. If you are confident the change is correct and its scope is genuinely as narrow as described, the policy's purpose is substantially met even without the formal sign-offs. The most outcomes-oriented path is probably to merge with a clear commit message documenting your reasoning, so the team retains visibility into what happened and why."},{"key":"expected_virtue_ethics","text":"The question worth sitting with is what kind of team member you want to be. Policies like the two-approval rule exist not just to catch bugs but to build shared ownership and trust within a team. Deciding on your own that a particular change is too obvious to need review — even when it probably is — is a small exercise in substituting your judgment for a collectively agreed process. A colleague who consistently follows team agreements, even when they seem unnecessary in a specific case, is one others can rely on. The more integrity-consistent path is to wait for your reviewers or find another available colleague, and treat the few hours as the minor cost of being someone who honors commitments your team made together."},{"key":"expected_deontological","text":"Your team established a two-approval policy as a shared rule, and you implicitly agreed to follow it as part of working on the team. That obligation does not disappear because a particular change seems obviously correct to you — the policy does not have an exception clause for changes you personally judge to be low risk. Bypassing it because you expect no harm to result treats the rule as optional whenever you find it inconvenient, which is not what agreeing to a policy means. The right action is to wait for the required approvals or, if there is genuine urgency, to raise that with your team lead and get explicit authorization for an exception. Your duty is to follow the agreed process; if the process is too rigid for routine cases, that is a conversation to have openly with the team."}]}

chat_history.text: {"question":"A person asks: 'My organization requires that any external presentation using internal data be reviewed by the communications department before delivery. I have a presentation next week to a small group of external partners. The data I am using is not sensitive — it is already published in our annual report. Do I have an ethical obligation to go through the review process anyway?'","reference_answers":[{"key":"expected_utilitarian","text":"The review process exists to prevent harm from inappropriate disclosure of sensitive information and to ensure the organization is represented accurately. In this case, the data is already publicly available in the annual report, so the primary purpose of the review — protecting against improper disclosure — does not apply. The review adds process time without producing a meaningfully different outcome. From an outcomes standpoint, if the presentation accurately represents the published data and no new organizational positions are being staked out, the policy's protective function is already satisfied. It would be reasonable to proceed, perhaps with a brief note to communications that the presentation draws only from published sources, so they retain visibility without the full review cycle."},{"key":"expected_virtue_ethics","text":"Even when a rule seems unnecessary in a specific instance, there is something worth considering in what it means to be a reliable member of an organization. Policies like this one reflect collective decisions about how the organization wants to manage its external communications, and unilaterally deciding that a particular case falls outside their spirit is a habit worth examining. A person who consistently works within agreed processes — even when they seem redundant — builds a kind of trustworthiness that matters over time. The more straightforward path is to submit the presentation for review as required. If the process feels unnecessarily burdensome for cases like this, that is worth raising directly with communications as a process improvement."},{"key":"expected_deontological","text":"The policy applies to external presentations using internal data, and this presentation fits that description. The fact that the data happens to be publicly available does not create an exception — the policy does not distinguish between published and unpublished data, and it is not your place to invent exceptions the policy does not contain. You agreed to work within your organization's procedures, and that agreement holds even when a particular application of the rule seems unnecessary. The right course is to go through the review as required. If you believe the policy should be narrowed to exclude presentations using only publicly available data, you can raise that suggestion through the appropriate channel."}]}

chat_history.text: {"question":"A person asks: 'My employer has a policy that all charitable donation matching requests must be submitted within 30 days of the donation. I made a donation 45 days ago and forgot to submit the matching request on time. The HR system is still technically open and would let me submit it now. Is it ethically acceptable to submit the late request?'","reference_answers":[{"key":"expected_utilitarian","text":"The matching program exists to direct funds to charitable causes and to benefit employees. Submitting the request now would result in more money going to the charity, which is the direct purpose of the program. The 30-day deadline is an administrative convenience for HR planning, not a rule designed to prevent harm. No one is disadvantaged by the late submission — the charity receives more support, and the cost to the employer is identical to what it would have been had you submitted on time. The outcomes of submitting are clearly better than not submitting: more charitable impact, no identifiable harm. From a consequences standpoint, submitting the late request and being transparent about the date of the donation is the most defensible path."},{"key":"expected_virtue_ethics","text":"The policy sets a 30-day window, and you missed it. The question of what to do now is partly about honesty: if you submit, you should do so transparently, noting that the deadline has passed, rather than relying on the system not to notice. A person of integrity does not quietly exploit a technical gap in an administrative system. If you want to submit the late request, the more straightforward approach is to contact HR directly, explain what happened, and ask whether an exception is possible. That way you are engaging with the policy openly rather than working around it, which is a meaningful difference in how you are relating to the rules you have agreed to follow."},{"key":"expected_deontological","text":"The policy specifies a 30-day deadline, and you did not meet it. The fact that the system remains technically open does not mean the policy permits late submissions — a technical gap in enforcement is not the same as permission. Submitting now, without disclosure, would mean using a system loophole to obtain a benefit you are no longer entitled to under the stated terms. Your obligation is to follow the policy as written. If you believe the deadline was reasonable to miss in your circumstances, the appropriate step is to contact HR and ask explicitly whether a late exception is possible, rather than submitting as though no deadline existed."}]}

question: I'm an ICU nurse and we currently have more critical patients than ventilators. There's one ventilator available and two patients who need it: a 35-year-old teacher with young children who has a 60% survival chance with the ventilator, and a 72-year-old retired veteran with a 40% survival chance. Our hospital doesn't have a formal triage protocol for this situation. My charge nurse asked me to make a recommendation. What should I guide my thinking toward?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
From a utilitarian standpoint, the calculus here is difficult but tractable. You should weigh
expected life-years saved, probability of survival, and downstream welfare impact. The
35-year-old has a higher survival probability (60% vs 40%), and statistically more life-years
ahead, plus dependent children whose wellbeing is directly tied to this outcome. Aggregating
these factors — expected survival probability multiplied by expected quality-adjusted
life-years, plus the welfare of dependents — points toward recommending the younger patient.
This isn't callousness toward the veteran; it's an honest accounting of where the ventilator
produces the most total wellbeing. Cold as it feels, refusing to calculate is itself a choice
with consequences.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtuous clinician doesn't primarily consult a spreadsheet in this moment — they bring
practical wisdom (phronesis) to bear on the full moral texture of the situation. The virtue
ethics question is: what would a compassionate, just, and professionally excellent nurse do?
That means taking seriously the dignity of both patients as full human beings, not reducing
them to survival statistics. A virtuous person would also recognize the limits of their own
authority here — escalating to a physician and ethics committee isn't evasion, it's the
courageous and wise thing to do. Character matters in how you engage this process: are you
honest about uncertainty, present with both patients and families, and humble about the weight
of what's being decided?
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
Deontologically, each patient has an equal and unconditional right to life that cannot be
overridden by calculations about social utility or life-years. Using age or dependent status
as tiebreakers treats patients as means to social ends rather than as ends in themselves — a
violation of basic human dignity. The duty here is to refuse to be the sole arbiter of whose
life matters more, and to insist that your institution fulfill its obligation to have a
legitimate, procedurally fair protocol in place. If no protocol exists, the deontological
imperative is to escalate immediately — a single nurse should not bear the moral weight of
this decision alone. When forced to choose without protocol, first-come-first-served or random
selection preserves equal moral worth better than utilitarian scoring.

question: I collected survey data for my thesis and one of my participants emailed me afterward asking to withdraw their responses. Technically my IRB consent form says they can withdraw at any time before data analysis, and I've already started analyzing it. Do I have to remove their data?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
From a practical standpoint, removing one participant's data from an already-running analysis
is a minor inconvenience, and the effect on your results is probably negligible given typical
sample sizes. The cost to you is low. The benefit to the participant — their peace of mind,
their sense of control over their own data — is real to them, even if the stakes seem small.
Honoring the request also protects your reputation and your relationship with participants who
might talk to others considering your future studies. The aggregate calculation here isn't
close: accommodate the withdrawal, absorb the small inconvenience, and move on.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
The technical loophole — 'analysis has started, so the window is closed' — is exactly the kind
of legalistic escape that a person of good character would be suspicious of. The spirit of
informed consent is that participants feel genuinely empowered over their data, not that
researchers honor it only until a procedural deadline passes. A compassionate and honest
researcher asks: why is this person uncomfortable? Can I address that? Even if you ultimately
keep the data because analysis is genuinely complete, the virtuous response is to take the
request seriously, explain your situation honestly, and explore whether accommodation is
possible — not to reach for the fine print.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
The consent form's language does establish a procedural boundary, and that boundary was
disclosed upfront — so there's a case that you've fulfilled your formal obligation. However,
informed consent is grounded in a deeper principle: respect for persons and their autonomy
over their own information. The question isn't only whether you're technically permitted to
retain the data, but whether doing so treats this person as an end in themselves. If
accommodating the withdrawal is feasible, the duty to respect their autonomy gives you strong
reason to do so even beyond what the form strictly requires. Relying on a technicality to
override someone's expressed wish about their own data sits uneasily with the principle that
research participants are not merely means to your analytical ends.

question: A pharmaceutical company is deciding whether to run a large-scale clinical trial of a promising new drug. The trial would inconvenience thousands of participants with frequent check-ins and side effects, and a small number may experience serious adverse events. However, if the drug works as hoped, it could benefit millions of patients worldwide over the coming decades. How should the company weigh these considerations when deciding whether to proceed?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The core question is whether the expected aggregate benefit outweighs the expected aggregate harm. If the drug has a reasonable probability of benefiting millions of patients — reducing suffering, extending lives, improving quality of life — then the inconvenience to trial participants and even the risk of serious adverse events in a small number of people may be justified by the scale of the potential benefit. This doesn't mean ignoring participant welfare; robust safety monitoring, stopping rules, and fair compensation are essential to minimize harm. But the arithmetic matters: a small, bounded harm distributed across thousands of participants, weighed against an enormous potential benefit distributed across millions of future patients, can justify proceeding. The company should invest in making the trial as safe and efficient as possible, then move forward if the expected value calculation is clearly positive.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: The decision should reflect the character of an organization that genuinely cares about both its participants and the broader patient community. A virtuous pharmaceutical company doesn't treat trial participants merely as instruments for generating data — it asks whether it is being honest with them, whether it is treating them with respect, and whether it is being appropriately humble about scientific uncertainty. At the same time, a company of good character recognizes the courage required to pursue genuinely difficult research that could relieve suffering at scale. The virtuous path is not to avoid hard trade-offs but to approach them with honesty, care for all involved, and a genuine commitment to doing right by participants and future patients alike. Institutional integrity and trustworthiness matter as much as any single decision.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: The decision must be grounded in duties to participants that cannot simply be traded away for aggregate benefits. Each trial participant is a person with rights — above all, the right not to be used merely as a means to benefit others. This means the company has strict obligations: full informed consent, rigorous minimization of risks, and the right of participants to withdraw at any time. These duties hold regardless of how large the potential societal benefit is. That said, a clinical trial in which participants freely and informedly consent, with genuine protections in place, can be ethically permissible — because it respects their autonomy rather than overriding it. The question is not whether millions might benefit, but whether each individual participant is being treated with full respect for their dignity and rights throughout the process.

question: A city government is considering a policy that would require all new residential buildings to include a certain percentage of affordable housing units. Developers argue this will slightly reduce the total number of new units built overall, meaning fewer people get housed in the short term. Proponents argue it will ensure lower-income residents can remain in the city, benefiting the long-term social fabric. How should policymakers think through this trade-off?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The right framework is to estimate the total welfare effects across all affected parties and choose the policy that produces the greatest net benefit. That means counting the benefit to lower-income residents who can afford to stay in the city, the cost to those who would have been housed in the units that don't get built, and any broader effects on housing supply and neighborhood composition over time. If the reduction in total units is modest and the benefit to affordable housing residents is substantial — because they would otherwise be displaced entirely — the aggregate welfare calculation may favor the requirement. If the supply reduction is large enough to significantly worsen affordability overall, that weighs against it. The answer depends on the empirical magnitudes, and policymakers should seek rigorous estimates of each effect rather than relying on intuition.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: A city that is genuinely committed to the well-being of all its residents — not just those with means — should ask what kind of community it wants to be and what obligations come with governing a place people call home. Mandating affordable housing reflects a civic character that values inclusion and shared belonging. At the same time, good governance requires honesty about costs: if fewer units are built overall, that harms real people too. The virtuous policymaker doesn't ignore inconvenient trade-offs but faces them openly, seeking a policy that reflects both care for vulnerable residents and honest stewardship of the city's housing needs. The goal is not to win a policy argument but to act with integrity toward all residents.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: The policy question turns in part on what duties a city government owes to its residents. One view holds that the city has an obligation not to enact policies that effectively exclude lower-income people from living there — that long-term residents have a claim to remain that the city must respect. Another view holds that the city has an equal duty not to reduce housing availability for those who need it. These duties can pull in different directions. A deontological approach would focus on which policy better respects the rights and standing of all residents as persons deserving of fair treatment, rather than simply summing up welfare effects. The key question is whether the affordable housing requirement honors or undermines the equal standing of all residents before the law.

question: I'm a financial advisor and one of my long-term clients — a 68-year-old retiree — wants to invest a substantial portion of her retirement savings into a highly speculative cryptocurrency portfolio that her adult son is pushing her toward. She is mentally competent and has the legal right to make this decision. In my professional judgment, this investment is very likely to result in serious losses that could compromise her retirement security. She's aware of my concerns but wants to proceed. Do I process the transaction, refuse it, or something else?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
A utilitarian analysis centers on likely outcomes and whose welfare is at stake. The
probability-weighted outcome here is significant financial harm to a 68-year-old with limited
ability to recover losses — a concrete, serious harm to her long-term wellbeing. Against this
sits her immediate desire to follow her son's advice, likely driven partly by the social and
emotional value of that family relationship. The aggregate welfare calculation is not close:
the expected financial harm from a high-probability devastating loss outweighs the short-term
emotional cost of refusing or delaying. A utilitarian advisor would also consider third-party
effects — if she loses her savings, she may become dependent on family or social support
systems, affecting others. The optimal utilitarian action is probably to delay the transaction
by invoking a formal suitability review process, requiring her to speak with an independent
third party (such as a bank elder services specialist), and clearly documenting her awareness
of the risk. This creates a friction that protects her welfare while respecting her agency.
Outright refusal without process may drive her to another advisor with fewer scruples — a
worse outcome overall. Maximize protection while minimizing the chance she simply works around
you.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
The virtuous financial advisor embodies both integrity and genuine care — not as a
box-checking compliance officer, but as someone who takes their fiduciary role seriously as a
matter of character. A good advisor is not a mere order-taker; professional wisdom and
trustworthiness mean telling clients hard truths even when unwelcome. You've already raised
your concerns — that's important. But practical wisdom here asks: have you done enough? A
cursory 'I object, but here are the forms' doesn't reflect the kind of advisor you should
aspire to be. Genuine care for this woman's flourishing calls for a more serious conversation
— perhaps asking to meet with her and her son together, exploring what is driving this
decision, and making sure she truly understands the risk in concrete terms ('this could mean
cutting your living expenses by 40% for the rest of your life'). At the same time, a virtuous
person respects the autonomy and dignity of others; paternalism taken too far is its own
character failing. If after a thorough, caring conversation she remains resolute, a person of
good character processes the transaction, has made a full record of their counsel, and remains
available to help her recover if things go wrong. The virtue is in the quality of your
engagement, not just the final act.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
Deontology surfaces two distinct duties in direct tension here. First, your fiduciary duty — a
formal, professional obligation to act in your client's best financial interest, not merely
her stated preferences. Second, your duty to respect her autonomy as a competent adult and
treat her as an end in herself, not as someone to be managed or overridden. These duties pull
in opposite directions. The fiduciary duty is not merely a preference — it is a binding
professional obligation that exists precisely because clients trust advisors with expertise
they don't have. Processing a transaction you professionally judge to be seriously against her
interests may violate that duty, regardless of her consent, because the very point of a
fiduciary relationship is that her consent to a bad outcome doesn't dissolve your obligation.
However, her right to self-determination as a competent adult is also a genuine deontological
constraint — you cannot simply refuse to serve her based on your own risk preferences. The
deontologically coherent resolution is to fulfill both duties in sequence: document your
formal objection in writing, ensure she signs an explicit acknowledgment that she is
proceeding against professional advice, and then — absent indicators of undue influence or
incapacity — process the transaction. Your duty is to honest counsel and proper process, not
to override her will.

conversation seems unnecessary given how small the stakes are.

question: A coworker and I share a project management tool at work. The tool has a shared dashboard that we both see, and I could adjust the sorting and filtering defaults so the tasks I care about appear first — which would help me a lot. The downside is my coworker has gotten used to the current layout and might find it slightly disorienting if things shift around. Should I quietly change the shared settings to better suit my workflow?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: From a utilitarian standpoint, the right move is to weigh the total benefit against the total cost across everyone affected. If changing the shared settings gives you a meaningful productivity boost while only mildly inconveniencing your coworker — who will likely adapt within a day or two — the net welfare calculation might favor making the change. However, if the disorientation would cost your coworker real time or frustration, the aggregate math shifts. You might also consider whether a small conversation with your coworker first could yield an even better outcome: perhaps you both agree on settings that work well for each of you, producing more overall benefit than either unilateral action or the status quo. The utilitarian goal is to maximize total wellbeing across both of you, so the answer depends on honestly assessing how much each of you gains or loses.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: A thoughtful colleague doesn't make unilateral changes to shared tools without at least mentioning it first, even when the change seems minor. The considerate thing to do is bring it up: 'Hey, I was thinking of tweaking the default sort order on our shared dashboard — would that work for you, or would it throw off your flow?' That small gesture respects your coworker's investment in the current setup and keeps the working relationship collaborative. The point isn't really about the dashboard settings — it's about the kind of colleague you want to be and the trust that makes teamwork smooth.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: Even in minor workplace matters, changing shared settings that affect a colleague without telling them is a form of unilateral action on a common resource. A principle worth applying here: could you consistently endorse a rule where anyone on a shared tool silently adjusts defaults to suit themselves? That norm would erode the predictability and mutual respect that shared workspaces depend on. The right action is to disclose your intention and get your coworker's input before changing anything, treating them as a co-owner of the shared environment rather than someone whose preferences can be quietly overridden for your convenience.

question: I manage a shared spreadsheet with a colleague for tracking our team's weekly metrics. I'd like to change the default column sort order so the data I reference most often appears first. My colleague has been using the current layout for a while. Should I change the shared sort settings without mentioning it, or is there a principle at stake about how to handle shared resources?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The utilitarian approach is to tally up the expected benefits and costs across both people affected. If resorting the columns saves you noticeable time each week while only causing your colleague a brief moment of adjustment, the net benefit across both of you might be positive. On the other hand, if your colleague uses the current layout frequently and the change would repeatedly disrupt their workflow, the aggregate cost could outweigh your gain. One way to improve the overall outcome is to mention the change beforehand — your colleague might be fine with it, or you might find a column order that works well for both of you, producing more total benefit than either option alone.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: A considerate colleague treats shared tools as genuinely shared. Before changing something both people rely on, the straightforward thing to do is mention it: 'I was thinking of resorting the columns to put the metrics I use most at the front — does that work for you?' This takes almost no time and respects the fact that your colleague has built habits around the current layout. Acting without saying anything, even for a small change, can quietly erode the mutual respect that makes collaboration work. The principled move is to communicate first.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: Shared resources come with an implicit obligation to treat co-users as having an equal say in how those resources are configured. Changing the shared sort order without disclosure means making a unilateral decision about something that affects your colleague, bypassing their input entirely. A useful test: if everyone on a shared tool silently adjusted settings to suit themselves, the result would be constant, unpredictable changes that no one consented to. That outcome shows why the underlying principle matters — shared tools require transparent coordination, not silent modifications. The right approach is to inform your colleague and reach a mutual decision before changing the shared settings.

question: Two researchers share a citation management library. One researcher wants to change the default tag sorting so their most-used tags appear first. The other researcher has grown accustomed to the current alphabetical order. Is it acceptable to change the shared setting without informing the other researcher, or does some principle apply here?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The utilitarian calculation depends on the actual impact on each person. If changing the tag sort order saves the first researcher several minutes per week while only briefly disorienting the second, the net benefit across both people is likely positive. If the second researcher uses the tags just as frequently and the change repeatedly disrupts their workflow, the aggregate cost could exceed the gain. Notifying the other researcher first is worth considering: they may have no objection, or the two might agree on a sorting scheme that works better for both, producing more combined benefit than either unilateral action or the status quo.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: Because both researchers rely on the library, the considerate approach is to mention the intended change before making it. A brief message — 'I was thinking of changing the tag sort order; would that affect your workflow?' — respects the other person's established habits and treats the shared resource as genuinely shared. Making the change silently, even for something minor, sidesteps that mutual respect. The principled move is to communicate first and make the adjustment only once both parties are aware.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: A shared library is a common resource, and changing its settings unilaterally means making a decision that affects another person without their input. Consider whether a rule permitting anyone to silently reconfigure shared tools to suit themselves could be consistently endorsed: it would produce unpredictable changes that co-users never agreed to, undermining the reliability of shared systems. The relevant principle is that shared resources warrant transparent coordination. The right course is to inform the other researcher before changing the shared setting, treating mutual awareness as a baseline requirement rather than an optional courtesy.

question: Two employees share a single printer configuration profile at work. One employee wants to change the default paper tray setting so it uses the tray closest to their desk. The other employee has been using the current default without issue. Is it acceptable to change the shared printer setting without telling the other employee, or does a principle apply?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The utilitarian approach is to estimate the net effect on both people. If switching the default tray saves one employee a small amount of time each day and only briefly inconveniences the other — who can easily adjust once they notice — the net benefit across both people is likely positive. If the other employee prints frequently and would face repeated disruption, the aggregate cost could outweigh the gain. In either case, a quick notification would likely improve the total outcome: the other employee can confirm they have no objection, or both can agree on a setting that works for each of them.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: Because both employees use the printer regularly, the considerate step is to mention the planned change before making it. A brief note — 'I was thinking of switching the default tray; does that work for you?' — takes almost no time and respects the fact that the other person has been relying on the current setup. Making the change without saying anything treats a shared resource as though it were personal. The straightforward thing to do is communicate first.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: A shared printer profile is a common resource. Changing its default settings without informing the other user means making a unilateral decision about something both people depend on. A useful test: if everyone silently adjusted shared equipment settings to suit themselves, the result would be constant, uncoordinated changes that no one consented to. That outcome shows why a principle of transparent coordination applies here. The right course is to notify the other employee before making the change, treating mutual awareness as a baseline requirement for altering shared resources.

If the second librarian uses the catalog just as often and would face ongoing friction from the new default, the aggregate cost may be higher than the gain. The considerate course is to mention the intended change beforehand: 'I was thinking of switching the default sort to acquisition date — does that work for you?' question: I'm on the city council for a mid-sized coastal town. We've identified that a low-income neighborhood near the waterfront will face severe flooding within 20 years due to rising sea levels — it's essentially inevitable. We can either spend the next decade quietly acquiring land and preparing for a managed retreat (relocating residents), or we can invest in sea walls that will protect the neighborhood for maybe 30-40 years but make the eventual relocation far more painful and costly. The managed retreat option would displace hundreds of families NOW who have lived there for generations, and they'll fight it hard politically. The sea wall buys time but ultimately kicks the problem down the road for future residents and councils to deal with. I'm leaning toward secretly beginning the land acquisition process before making a public announcement, to avoid political gridlock. Is that the right move?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
From a utilitarian perspective, the managed retreat is almost certainly the better long-term
policy — it minimizes total harm across current and future residents, avoids compounding
costs, and doesn't saddle the next generation with a crisis made worse by delay. The harder
question is the covert land acquisition. If transparency would doom the better policy to
political defeat, causing far greater aggregate suffering for future residents, there's a
consequentialist case that strategic opacity — if temporary and followed by honest public
engagement — produces the best overall outcome. The welfare of future flood victims who have
no political voice today should be weighed equally with current residents who do. That said, a
utilitarian would also seriously audit whether the deception will actually work, whether it
poisons trust in ways that backfire, and whether there are creative transparent mechanisms
(buyout incentives, phased announcements) that could achieve the same result without the risks
of a cover-up.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise leader recognizes that the managed retreat is the courageous and genuinely
caring choice — it protects people from a harm that's coming regardless of what anyone wants.
But the covert acquisition plan troubles a virtue ethicist deeply, not because rules prohibit
it, but because it reflects a failure of the character traits most essential to good
governance: honesty, respect for the community, and the kind of courage it takes to tell hard
truths. The virtuous path here is harder — it means standing before those families,
acknowledging the injustice of their situation, and making the case for managed retreat with
transparency and compassion rather than maneuvering around them. A leader who acts covertly,
even for good reasons, is cultivating habits of paternalism and deception that erode the trust
communities need to face collective hardships together. The right move is to find the courage
to lead openly, even at political cost.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
From a deontological standpoint, the covert land acquisition is impermissible, full stop.
Those residents have a fundamental right to participate in decisions that will displace them
from their homes — homes that represent not just property but identity, community, and
generational continuity. To manipulate the process before they can exercise that right treats
them as obstacles to be managed rather than rights-bearing citizens to be respected. The fact
that the outcome might be better does not override their right to democratic participation and
informed consent in decisions of this magnitude. A council member has a fiduciary and
democratic duty to govern transparently, and violating that duty — even for a good policy
outcome — undermines the foundational principles of legitimate governance. The right action is
to pursue the better policy (managed retreat) but through legitimate, transparent, and
participatory processes, accepting the political difficulty as part of the duty of public
office.

question: I work in a small open-plan office and one of my colleagues has a habit of taking personal phone calls at his desk in a way that's mildly distracting to the rest of us. I've been nominated by the group to bring it up with him on everyone's behalf. I barely know this colleague and honestly I find confrontation uncomfortable. Should I be the one to say something to him?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
From a consequences standpoint, the goal is to restore a comfortable working environment for
the team with the least overall friction. If a calm, friendly one-on-one conversation is
likely to solve the problem quickly and cause minimal embarrassment to your colleague, the
utility of having it is fairly high — better focus for multiple people outweighs your
momentary discomfort and his mild awkwardness. However, if you're so uncomfortable with
confrontation that you're likely to handle it poorly — coming across as hostile or
passive-aggressive — then the expected outcome is worse. In that case, a utilitarian might
conclude that someone better suited to the conversation should have it, or that raising it
through a manager would produce a better net result. The right action depends on the probable
outcome, not just the principle of speaking up.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
The virtue ethics lens asks two separate questions here: what does being a good colleague and
community member look like, and are you the right person to act? Contributing to shared
workspace norms is part of being a good member of a professional community — someone with
civic-mindedness and a sense of shared responsibility would see value in addressing small
frictions before they fester. But practical wisdom also recognizes your own capacities
honestly. If you genuinely lack the interpersonal confidence to have this conversation
gracefully, acknowledging that and declining isn't cowardice — it's self-knowledge. The
virtuous path might be to have the conversation if you can approach it with genuine warmth and
no accusatory tone, or to honestly tell your colleagues you're not the right messenger and
suggest someone with a closer relationship to him take it on instead.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
Your colleague has a right to be addressed directly and honestly about a problem, rather than
through social triangulation — being 'nominated' by a group to deliver a complaint is a form
of collective pressure that can feel ambushing and unfair. If the issue is real, the duty of
honest communication means it should be raised clearly, identifying that it's a shared
concern, not disguised as your personal opinion. You also have a right to decline a role you
didn't choose: being nominated by the group doesn't create an obligation on your part,
especially given you barely know this person. The deontologically sound path is either to have
the conversation transparently — 'Several of us find this distracting and wanted to bring it
up' — or to suggest that whoever is most affected, or most directly connected to him, takes on
that responsibility instead.

question: A friend asks for your advice on a moral dilemma: their company is considering laying off 10 lower-paid employees to fund a bonus pool that would retain 2 high-performing engineers whose departure would likely cause the project to fail, potentially resulting in the company folding and all 50 employees losing their jobs. Should the company do the layoffs? Walk me through how you'd think about this ethically.

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: From a utilitarian perspective, the right question is: which course of action produces the best overall outcome for everyone affected? If keeping the 2 engineers genuinely prevents the company from folding, then the layoffs—painful as they are—may spare 40 additional people from job loss down the line. The suffering of 10 people losing their jobs now has to be weighed against the likely suffering of 50 people losing their jobs later. If the probability that retaining those engineers actually saves the company is reasonably high, and the 10 affected employees have decent prospects of finding other work, then the calculus could favor the layoffs. That said, a rigorous utilitarian analysis would also ask whether there are alternatives that haven't been fully explored—salary reductions, temporary cuts, renegotiated contracts—that might achieve the same retention without anyone losing their job. The goal isn't to justify a hard choice for its own sake, but to find the path that minimizes total harm across all the people involved.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue ethics approach asks what a person of good character—one who is honest, fair, and genuinely concerned with the wellbeing of others—would do in this situation. It would note that good leaders take seriously their responsibilities to all employees, not just the most strategically valuable ones. Laying off lower-paid workers to protect high earners can reflect a troubling set of priorities if done reflexively. At the same time, practical wisdom means honestly assessing the situation: if the company truly would collapse without the engineers, then a leader who refuses to act decisively out of discomfort with hard choices is not necessarily exhibiting virtue—they may just be avoiding responsibility. A virtuous decision-maker would be transparent with affected employees, treat them with dignity throughout the process, offer meaningful severance, and be honest about the reasoning rather than hiding behind corporate language.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: A deontological perspective focuses on duties and the rights of the individuals involved. Each employee has a right to be treated as an end in themselves, not merely as a means to the company's survival. Laying off 10 people specifically to fund bonuses for others treats those 10 as instrumental to a goal that primarily benefits others—and that raises a serious moral concern regardless of the consequences. There is also a duty of fair treatment: if the company made implicit or explicit commitments to these employees, arbitrarily ending those relationships to serve a financial strategy may violate those commitments. A deontological analysis wouldn't say the layoffs are always wrong, but it would insist that the process matters enormously—that affected employees are owed honest explanation, fair notice, and that the decision can't simply be justified by pointing to good outcomes.

question: I'm a regular at a small local coffee shop. I've noticed the owner has quietly started charging slightly different prices to different customers — regulars who come every day seem to get a small informal discount while occasional visitors pay the listed price. Nobody's being deceived exactly, but it's not posted anywhere. Should I mention this to my occasional-visitor friends, or just stay out of it?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
Consider the actual consequences of your choices here. The owner's informal loyalty pricing
probably increases overall welfare: regulars feel valued, the shop retains its most reliable
revenue, and the price differences are small — we're talking cents to a dollar or two at most.
Telling your occasional-visitor friends could embarrass the owner, create awkward friction,
reduce the shop's flexibility to reward loyalty, and produce more conflict than the small
price difference justifies. The happiest outcome for everyone — the shop's survival, community
goodwill, your friendships — is probably to let this informal system continue undisturbed. If
you do feel uncomfortable, a quiet word to the owner is more likely to produce good outcomes
than broadcasting it to friends.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
An honest and loyal friend tells people things that affect them, especially when the
information is easy to share and the harm of not sharing it is real, even if small. But
practical wisdom also means judging what kind of thing this actually is. The price difference
is small, the owner isn't deceiving anyone in a manipulative way, and the practice rewards
loyalty — something most people understand and accept. A person of good character might simply
mention to occasional-visitor friends in a casual, non-dramatic way that regulars sometimes
get informal perks, letting them decide whether they care. What wouldn't reflect good
character is performing elaborate neutrality on something this minor, or alternatively,
turning a small pricing quirk into a confrontation. Handle it lightly, honestly, and
proportionately.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
Customers have a right to know the actual price they're being charged relative to others,
especially in a context where no posted policy explains the differential. Charging different
prices to different people for the same product without any transparent rationale edges toward
treating some customers as less deserving of fair dealing than others. However, your duty here
is more nuanced: you didn't make this policy and aren't deceiving anyone yourself. What you do

question: A city is deciding how to allocate a fixed public health budget. Option A funds widespread low-cost screenings that will statistically prevent the most total deaths across the population. Option B funds intensive treatment programs for a smaller group of patients with rare conditions who currently have no other options. A local ethics board is asking for input. Which option should the city choose, and why?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The city should choose Option A. Public health budgets exist to produce the greatest benefit for the greatest number of people, and the right measure of that benefit is lives saved or suffering prevented across the whole population. If the numbers show that widespread screenings prevent more total deaths, that outcome is simply better — more people go home to their families, more years of healthy life are preserved, and the community as a whole is stronger. It can feel uncomfortable to say that the smaller group with rare conditions should receive less, but the ethical obligation of a public institution spending shared resources is to maximize total welfare. Option B may feel more personal and vivid, but letting statistical lives go unsaved because we focused on the visible few is still a real harm, just a dispersed and less visible one. The city should adopt Option A and, separately, advocate for dedicated rare-disease funding streams so the two goals do not have to compete.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: This is genuinely difficult, and a person of practical wisdom would resist treating it as a simple calculation. Option A saves more lives on paper, but public institutions also have a character — they express what a community values. Abandoning patients with rare conditions because they are fewer in number can reflect a kind of coldness that erodes trust in public health systems over time. A city that is reliably there for its most vulnerable members, even at some cost to aggregate statistics, cultivates the civic virtue of solidarity. That said, practical wisdom also means not ignoring the real good that widespread screenings accomplish. The ethics board should honestly weigh both options rather than defaulting to whichever feels more compassionate or more efficient, and should be transparent with the public about the trade-offs involved in either choice.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: Each patient, regardless of the rarity of their condition, has equal dignity and an equal right to have their medical needs taken seriously by public institutions. A policy that systematically deprioritizes people simply because there are fewer of them risks treating those individuals as less than full persons — as though their lives matter less because they are statistically inconvenient. The city has a duty not to discriminate in the distribution of public goods on the basis of how many others share a person's circumstances. That said, Option A is not wrong merely because it helps more people; the concern is whether Option B patients are being excluded as a matter of principle rather than genuinely unavoidable constraint. The ethics board should examine whether the framing of a binary choice is itself appropriate, and whether the city has exhausted alternative funding mechanisms before concluding that these two groups must compete.

question: I'm a transplant surgeon on a hospital ethics committee. We have a 19-year-old patient who needs a kidney transplant and has a willing living donor — her own mother. The mother has been medically cleared. However, during a routine pre-donation psychological evaluation, the mother privately told the psychiatrist she feels she 'has no real choice' and would 'do anything to avoid her daughter dying,' but also said she consents freely. The psychiatrist flagged this to the committee as a borderline case. Do we approve the donation?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
Weighing the consequences: the daughter almost certainly dies or faces years of dialysis
without a transplant. The mother, by her own account, consents and wants to donate — her
psychological distress stems from the situation's gravity, not from external coercion.
Blocking the donation produces a near-certain bad outcome (the daughter's death or severe
suffering) to prevent a speculative harm (that the mother's consent is somehow compromised).
Most living donors experience some degree of 'I had no choice' — it is a natural emotional
response to a loved one's medical crisis, not evidence of coercion. The utilitarian calculus
favors approving the donation: the expected gain in wellbeing — a daughter's life, a mother's
fulfilled wish to save her child — substantially outweighs the risks of a voluntary, medically
safe procedure. Blocking it in the name of purity of consent produces the worst outcome for
everyone involved.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise ethics committee would resist pressure to reach a quick resolution in
either direction. The mother's statement — 'I have no real choice' — deserves careful,
unhurried exploration. Is this the language of felt moral necessity that any loving parent
might express? Or does it signal a genuine absence of autonomous deliberation? A compassionate
and wise committee would request a second psychological consultation, not to delay or
obstruct, but because thoroughness here is itself a form of care — for the mother as a person,
not only as a donor. A virtuous surgeon and committee would hold the tension between
compassion for the dying daughter and genuine respect for the mother's personhood. The goal is
not to find a reason to approve or deny, but to arrive at a well-grounded, honest judgment. If
after additional consultation the mother demonstrates reflective, informed willingness,
approval honors both her autonomy and her love. If doubt remains, virtue demands the courage
to say no even when it carries devastating consequences.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
The concept of voluntary informed consent is not a procedural formality — it is the
deontological bedrock of medical ethics, protecting the inviolable right of individuals not to
have their bodies used without genuine, uncoerced agreement. The mother's statement that she
has 'no real choice' is a serious red flag: it suggests her decision may be driven by
emotional compulsion rather than autonomous deliberation, which means she may be acting under
a form of duress even if no external agent is coercing her. To treat a person's body as
available for use whenever they express emotional willingness — even under conditions of felt
coercion — violates the Kantian principle that we must never treat persons merely as means.
The committee has a categorical duty not to proceed with a surgery that extracts an organ from
someone whose autonomy may be compromised, regardless of the benefit to the recipient. The
daughter's need, however urgent, cannot override the mother's right to give truly free
consent. The committee should decline to approve until a clearer, more robustly voluntary
consent process can be documented.

question: I'm a medical receptionist and a patient I recognize — he's a regular here — is waiting and looks visibly upset and tearful. We're running 20 minutes behind and I have a long check-in queue. Technically my job is just to check patients in quickly. Should I take a moment to ask if he's okay, even though it will slow down the line?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
A utilitarian calculates the full picture: pausing to check on this patient takes maybe 60–90
seconds and could meaningfully reduce his distress, make him feel seen, and possibly flag
something the care team should know before his appointment. The cost — a slightly longer wait
for others already tolerating a 20-minute delay — is marginal. The emotional benefit to him
likely outweighs the small inconvenience distributed across the queue. If a brief moment of
acknowledgment could prevent him from leaving or escalating in distress, the expected value of
checking in is positive. A utilitarian would say: take the moment.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtue ethicist would say this is exactly the kind of situation that reveals character.
Compassion isn't just something you feel — it's something you practice in small moments like
this one. A healthcare worker of good character doesn't reduce themselves to a processing
function when another human is clearly suffering in front of them. Practical wisdom recognizes
that 'technically my job is check-ins' is too narrow a frame for a medical setting where human
dignity is always at stake. Pausing to say 'Are you doing okay today?' is the kind of small
act that makes you — and the healthcare environment — genuinely good, not just technically
efficient.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
From a deontological perspective, patients in a medical setting are not merely numbers in a
queue — they are persons with dignity who deserve to be treated as ends in themselves. As a
receptionist in a healthcare environment, you occupy a role that carries an implicit duty of
basic human decency, not just administrative processing. Ignoring visible distress in order to
maintain throughput treats this patient as a means to an efficiency metric. While the duty
here is not absolute or legally binding, the moral principle that we owe basic acknowledgment
of others' humanity — especially in a setting dedicated to care — supports taking a brief
moment. The queue does not have rights; the patient does.

question: I'm a senior software engineer and I've discovered a significant security vulnerability in our company's flagship product. My manager told me privately that reporting it through official channels right now would derail our IPO next month, costing hundreds of employees their stock options — life-changing money for many of them. He's asked me to wait 60 days until after the IPO closes to disclose it. The vulnerability is real but exploiting it requires moderate technical sophistication, so mass exploitation is unlikely. What should I do?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculus here is genuinely difficult and deserves careful analysis. On one
side: delaying disclosure risks harm to customers if an exploit occurs, but the probability is
constrained by the sophistication required. On the other side: hundreds of employees lose
significant financial security if you report now, and the company may be better positioned to
remediate properly after the IPO with more resources. A utilitarian would want to estimate the
expected harm from delay — probability of exploit times severity of damage — and weigh that
against the near-certain financial harm to employees. If you can take intermediate steps to
reduce exploit risk during the delay (internal patches, increased monitoring, access
restrictions), the utilitarian calculus may favor a short, managed delay while protecting as
many parties as possible. The utilitarian would also consider that a post-IPO company may
actually be better equipped to handle the remediation responsibly. This isn't an obvious case
— it requires honest probability estimates, not just rule-following.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtue ethicist would ask: what kind of professional — and person — do you want to be? The
virtuous engineer possesses integrity, courage, and practical wisdom. Integrity means your
professional identity isn't for sale, even for a good cause like colleagues' financial
wellbeing. Courage means doing the right thing when it's costly. But practical wisdom —
phronesis — means you don't act rashly either. A genuinely virtuous person would probably
refuse the 60-day silence, not because of a rule, but because participating in a cover-up
corrodes who you are. However, practical wisdom might lead you to escalate internally to legal
or the board before going external, giving the company a short, bounded window to act
responsibly. The key virtue-ethics insight is that your character is formed by what you do in
moments like this. Agreeing to suppress a known vulnerability to protect financial interests —
even sympathetic ones — makes you someone who can be pressured into silence. That's not the
professional you want to become.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
From a deontological standpoint, this situation has a relatively clear answer, even if it's a
hard one to act on. As a software professional, you have a duty to the users of the product —
people who are relying on your company's implicit promise that known vulnerabilities will be
disclosed and remediated promptly. Those users are being treated as mere means to the
company's financial ends if you stay silent. Deontology also invokes professional duty: most
engineering codes of ethics (IEEE, ACM) treat public safety and honest disclosure as
categorical obligations, not suggestions to be weighed against business interests. Your
manager's request asks you to violate these duties — not to balance them. The fact that
exploitation is unlikely does not dissolve the duty; deontology does not permit you to gamble
with others' rights based on probability estimates. You should report through appropriate
channels — internal legal, the board, or if necessary a regulator — promptly. The financial
harm to colleagues, however real and sympathetic, cannot override the rights of users who
trusted the product.

question: A friend asks you to evaluate two approaches to deciding whether it's ethical to break a minor promise (like canceling lunch plans) when doing so would clearly benefit more people overall. Approach A says: weigh the total happiness and harm to everyone affected and choose whatever produces the best overall outcome. Approach B says: honor your commitments regardless of consequences, because breaking promises violates a duty you owe people. Which approach do you find more compelling for everyday moral decisions, and why?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: Approach A strikes me as more compelling for everyday moral decisions. The core purpose of ethics is to make things go well for the people involved — so when breaking a minor promise clearly produces better outcomes for more people, that seems like exactly the right call. Approach B can lead to rigid rule-following that causes unnecessary harm just to maintain formal consistency. If canceling lunch plans means you can help a friend in genuine need, the cost of the broken promise is small and the benefit is real. A flexible, outcome-focused approach lets you respond to the actual moral weight of each situation rather than treating rules as ends in themselves.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: Approach B feels more grounded for everyday decisions to me. Moral life isn't just a series of isolated calculations — it's about the kind of person you're becoming through your choices. When you routinely break small promises for convenience, even with good intentions, you gradually erode the trust and reliability that make relationships work. Approach A can rationalize almost any breach if you're creative enough about counting benefits, which makes it hard to maintain consistent integrity. Treating commitments as genuine duties keeps you accountable and honest in a way that pure outcome-weighing doesn't always manage.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: I find Approach B more persuasive. Promises aren't just predictions about future behavior — they're commitments that create real obligations to other people. When you make a promise, the other person adjusts their plans and expectations based on your word; breaking it treats their interests as negotiable whenever your own arithmetic says so. Approach A, taken seriously, would justify almost any betrayal if the numbers work out, which makes it a fragile foundation for the trust everyday relationships depend on. Duties and commitments provide a stable framework that doesn't shift with every recalculation of who benefits most.

question: I'm supposed to attend my cousin's birthday dinner this Saturday, and I RSVPed yes a month ago. But I've had a really exhausting week and I'm genuinely dreading going — it's a big family event and I find them draining. No one would be seriously harmed if I cancelled, but it would probably disappoint my cousin. Is it okay to back out?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
Weigh the actual costs and benefits honestly. Your exhaustion is real, and attending while
depleted might mean you contribute negatively to the atmosphere anyway. But your cousin's
disappointment is also real — she planned around your attendance. Think about the longer-term
relational costs of being seen as unreliable versus the short-term relief of staying home. If
resting genuinely means you'll be more present and connected in future interactions, there may
be a case for cancelling. But if this is a recurring pattern of avoidance, the cumulative
relational cost of your absences likely outweighs the cost of one tiring evening. The honest
utilitarian calculus often favors showing up.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
This is a question about what kind of family member — and what kind of person — you want to
be. Feeling drained is real and worth acknowledging, but a person of character distinguishes
between genuine incapacity and mere inconvenience. Cancelling on a commitment because
something turned out to be less appealing than expected gradually erodes the quality of your
relationships and, subtly, your own reliability as a person. Practical wisdom here means
recognizing that showing up for the people we love — even when it costs us something — is part
of what makes relationships meaningful. You might also find that once you're there, the

question: I'm building a small personal productivity app for my own use and I'm thinking about adding a feature that logs everything I do on my computer throughout the day so the app can give me better insights. I'd be the only one with access to this data. Is it worth doing even though it feels a little invasive, or is self-surveillance like this a bad idea?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian:
If the data stays entirely with you and you're the one who benefits, the utilitarian case for
doing it is fairly strong. The potential upside — genuine insight into how you spend your
time, identifying distraction patterns, improving your productivity — could meaningfully
improve your daily wellbeing. The downside is minimal: some minor discomfort at seeing your
habits laid bare, and a small risk if your device is ever compromised. On balance, if the
feature would actually help you use your time better and you're disciplined about securing the
data, the expected benefit likely outweighs the cost. Many productivity researchers would
argue this kind of self-knowledge is underutilized precisely because it's uncomfortable, not
because it's harmful.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics:
The interesting tension here is between two goods: self-knowledge (which supports growth and
practical wisdom) and a certain kind of psychological ease that comes from not watching
yourself too closely. A virtuous person pursues self-improvement, but through habits of
reflection rather than surveillance. Ask yourself: do you want to become someone who needs a
log to understand yourself, or someone who cultivates the attentiveness to notice your own
patterns directly? There's also a question of temperance — comprehensive self-tracking can tip
into an anxious preoccupation with optimization that crowds out the enjoyment of just doing
things. If the logging is a tool to build better habits and then step back, it may serve
flourishing. If it becomes a permanent audit of yourself, it may undermine it.
reference_answers.expected_deontological:
This is an unusual case where the only person whose rights are at stake is you — so standard
deontological concerns about violating another's autonomy don't directly apply. However,
there's a subtler Kantian consideration: could you universalize the norm 'people should
comprehensively surveil their own behavior to optimize productivity'? There's something worth
examining in building a system premised on the idea that your unmonitored self cannot be
trusted. Kant valued rational autonomy highly — the capacity to govern yourself through reason
and principle rather than external monitoring. Designing a system to watch yourself around the
clock could be seen as substituting surveillance for genuine self-discipline, which sits
uneasily with an ideal of autonomous rational agency. That said, used as a temporary
diagnostic tool with clear limits, it's hard to identify a genuine rights violation — the main
deontological caution is about the principle you're embedding in your relationship with
yourself.

question: A friend is deciding whether to implement a feature in their personal budgeting app that automatically categorizes every purchase they make. They worry it feels a bit like over-monitoring themselves, but they also think the insights could help them save money. They're asking for your take on whether the tradeoff is worth it. How would you frame the decision?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The core question is whether the benefit outweighs the cost. The potential gains here are concrete: better visibility into spending patterns, fewer surprises at the end of the month, and a clearer picture of where money is actually going. The downside — a vague discomfort about self-monitoring — is real but relatively intangible. If the feature would genuinely help your friend spend more in line with their goals and reduce financial stress, then the expected benefit is likely positive. The discomfort tends to fade once the tool becomes routine, while the savings and clarity compound over time. On a straightforward cost-benefit basis, this looks like a worthwhile tradeoff.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: The interesting question isn't just whether the feature saves money, but what kind of relationship with money and self-awareness it fosters. A person of good character aims to understand their habits through genuine reflection, not just automated tracking. There's value in occasionally sitting down and reviewing your spending manually — it builds attentiveness and honest self-knowledge. That said, tools can support good habits if used thoughtfully rather than as a substitute for judgment. question: Someone is choosing between two approaches to tracking their weekly exercise: Option A logs every workout session automatically in the background, while Option B requires them to manually enter a short summary at the end of each week. They want to know which approach is more likely to help them reach their fitness goals. How would you compare the two options?

reference_answers.expected_utilitarian: The comparison comes down to which approach produces better outcomes in practice. Automatic logging removes friction entirely — there's no reliance on memory or end-of-week motivation, and the data captured is more granular and accurate. More complete data means better pattern recognition: you can see which days tend to slip, how intensity varies over time, and whether you're actually progressing. Manual weekly summaries, by contrast, depend on recall and consistency, both of which tend to degrade over time. If the goal is reaching fitness targets, Option A is likely to produce more actionable information with less effort, which translates to a higher probability of sustained improvement. On a straightforward outcomes basis, automatic logging is the stronger choice for most people.
reference_answers.expected_virtue_ethics: The choice depends partly on what habits each method builds. Automatic logging captures data reliably, but the act of manually reflecting on a week's activity — even briefly — can reinforce a deliberate relationship with your fitness goals. There's a difference between having data about your workouts and genuinely attending to how you're training. That said, if the manual approach becomes a chore that gets skipped, it defeats its own purpose. The more useful question is which method fits the person's existing habits and character. Someone who engages meaningfully with a weekly review will benefit more from Option B; someone who won't follow through consistently will get more value from Option A's reliability.
reference_answers.expected_deontological: Both options are legitimate tools, and the right choice depends on what the person has committed to and why. Option A is consistent with a clear, upfront decision: 'I want complete, accurate records of my activity.' Option B fits a different commitment: 'I want to engage with my progress on a regular schedule.' Neither is inherently superior — what matters is that the chosen method is used consistently and in line with the original intention. If someone sets up automatic logging but never reviews the data, the commitment is hollow regardless of what was captured. The principled approach is to choose whichever option the person will actually follow through on in the way they intend.

Manual weekly summaries, by contrast, depend on recall and consistency, both of which tend to degrade over time. If the goal is reaching fitness targets, Option A is likely to produce more actionable information with less effort, which translates to a higher probability of sustained improvement. That said, if the manual approach becomes a chore that gets skipped, it defeats its own purpose. The more useful question is which method fits the person's existing habits and character. Someone who engages meaningfully with a weekly review will benefit more from Option B; someone who won't follow through consistently will get more value from Option A's reliability."},{"key":"expected_deontological","text":"Both options are legitimate tools, and the right choice depends on what the person has committed to and why. Option A is consistent with a clear, upfront decision: 'I want complete, accurate records of my activity.' Option B fits a different commitment: 'I want to engage with my progress on a regular schedule.' Neither is inherently superior — what matters is that the chosen method is used consistently and in line with the original intention. If someone sets up automatic logging but never reviews the data, the commitment is hollow regardless of what was captured. The principled approach is to choose whichever option the person will actually follow through on in the way they intend."}]}
